newsitem.title: PERU: Peru sees late Feb, March formal hostage talks.
newsitem.headline: Peru sees late Feb, March formal hostage talks.

text.p: Peru's President Alberto Fujimori said on Tuesday the resumption of preliminary talks with Marxist rebels to end the Lima hostage crisis may lead to formal negotiations in late February or March.

"Hopefully, by the end of February or in March the negotiating commission will be in place," Fujimori, who was in London, told Peruvian radio. He also told a news conference he was negotiating with other countries that may be willing to grant asylum to Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels, who have been holding 72 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima for nearly two months.

He told the packed news conference he may approach Cuba, whose 1959 revolution inspired the MRTA, about asylum possibilities. "I have not yet had any contact with Cuba. (President) Fidel Castro is a personal friend ... if necessary I'll make a call to Fidel Castro. Why not?" he said.

Fujimori, who on Monday won British Prime Minister John Major's support for a peaceful solution to the crisis, was to meet on Tuesday with former Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher before catching a late-night flight home.

In Lima, hopes ran high ahead of the preliminary direct talks, despite the seemingly irreconcilable positions dividing the government and the MRTA hostage-takers. "I do believe we are entering the home stretch," Peru's public defender, Jorge Santistevan de Noriega, told local television.

But the talks promised to be tough. The MRTA, which stormed the envoy's compound on Dec. 17, said it would not drop its main demand of freedom for more than 400 jailed comrades. Fujimori in London again flatly rejected that possibility as well as the payment of ransom.

"The beginning of talks does not necessarily mean the start of a solution to the conflict," rebel leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini said on Monday via walkie-talkie. He expressed the MRTA's "total willingness" to restart talks but accused Fujimori of seeking to use the talks as a "psychological weapon," charging that he had issued a "veiled threat" to use force against the rebels if negotiations fail.

No starting time or agenda were given for the talks between government negotiator Domingo Palermo and No. 2 rebel Roli Rojas, a 34-year-old former transport worker who goes by the nom de guerre "El Arabe" - The Arab.
On Monday, an explosion and burst of automatic weapons fire underscored the hair-trigger atmosphere at the residence in Lima's upscale San Isidro district.

Police initially said an animal had stepped on a landmine planted by rebels at the compound. Rebels later said they had tossed a grenade and fired shots in response to provocations by police special forces and sharphooters surrounding the compound. Nobody was hurt in the incident.
Rebels and the government last met face to face on Dec. 28, after which talks deadlocked over Fujimori's refusal even to discuss the MRTA's principal demand.
The Red Cross on Monday readied final details for the renewed talks to be held at a house across the street.
